utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'd like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused, and everyone else. We'll be resuming at the hearing of the witness who appeared yesterday. I'd also like to greet the witness, who is here, and I will give the floor to Mr. Scott to continue with his examination-in-chief. So far I think he has already taken up about two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Yes -- one never knows, of course, but I don't contemplate any problems in finishing the witness within the schedule that we had indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Idrizovic.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we finished yesterday, we were approaching the end of 1992 and I would like to finish 1992 rather quickly this morning, and if we could then move on to 1993. Can you tell the Judges at the end of November of 1992 was there -- was there a blockage of a particular check-point that affected the ability of the Jablanica TO or ABiH to receive logistical support?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, where did you during this -- not you, excuse me. Did the Jablanica army unit of the Bosnia-Herzegovina [sic] receive most of its logistical support during this time-period from Visoko?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did anything happen in November 1992 to break or disrupt your connection to the logistical base in Visoko?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Something happened in Kiseljak. A group of logistics men went to take charge of some equipment that we needed to raise the blockade of Sarajevo. This was a plan that was being prepared in December 1992. Unfortunately, the men were detained, the equipment was taken from them, and three or four days later they were released. The equipment wasn't returned, and that was the last time that we were able to obtain some equipment from the logistics base in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Who stopped these men and where?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were stopped at an HVO check-point in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Also at the end of November of 1992, sir, were you invited to a meeting or was a meeting proposed to you with Slobodan Praljak?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in November. How should I put it? There was intense activity in connection with the events in Prozor. We only barely managed to secure some kind of peace in Jablanica because refugees from Prozor requested that we expel the Croats, that we treat them in an inhumane way, and for this reason I personally had quite a few problems with them. At one point in time they wrote to the Supreme Command staff and said that we had crossed over to the HVO side because we wouldn't help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Wouldn't help who, sir, just so the record is clear?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Help these refugees from Prozor. At the time Mr. Praljak would appear as well as Mr. Izetbegovic, men of ours from the Supreme Command staff would come, the corps command and Mr. Pasalic would come and many others. Activities were carried out almost on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, sir, before we go back to the meeting -- I want to proceed step by step, if we can. Before we go back to the possibility of this meeting with Mr. Praljak, you say that there was concern about feelings expressed by some of the Muslim refugees coming from Prozor to Jablanica about the Croats that were in Jablanica. Can you tell the Judges, please, were any of the Croat residents of Jablanica ever expelled out of their flats in Jablanica to make room for Muslim refugees?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one was ever expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that something that you directly and personally were involved in, that is, if you will, maintaining the peace between the Croats and Muslims in Jablanica town?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two things. There was a headquarters for the accommodation of refugees in the municipality. Members of the military didn't have time to deal with accommodation for refugees. At the time my cooperation with the HVO commander, Mr. Marko Zelenika, was very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go back, then, to the meeting with Mr. Praljak. Were you invited or was it suggested to you that you meet with Mr. Praljak in Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we have two things here that are not related. Mr. Praljak came to a meeting, and on that occasion I was the host. The discussion concerned the possibility of the return of the Muslims from Prozor to Jablanica in order to calm down the situation in Jablanica. Some of them were prepared to return. The purpose of the meeting with Mr. Praljak and his associates was to return the refugees from Jablanica to Prozor. And the second issue you mentioned -- well, in November --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, let me stop you there. Excuse me, sir. Again, please, let's go step by step. So there was a first meeting with Mr. Praljak to talk about the return of Muslims, the Muslims that had left Prozor, to return those Muslim refugees to Prozor, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's finish on that before we go on to the next meeting. What was the result of that. During that time-period, during November, December, or so, 1992, were the Muslims allowed to return to Prozor?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, would you go to the second meeting, then, that you started to tell --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very important issue and requires clarification. You say that you met Mr. Praljak in connection with the return of the Muslims who had left Prozor and who were in Jablanica and who were supposed to return to Prozor, and you said that they didn't return to Prozor. What I would like to know, since it's important for us, is: What was Mr. Praljak's position at the meeting? What did he say? What did he want? What did he actually do to ensure that these Muslims could return to Prozor? Do you have any precise information that you could provide us with? When was this meeting held and who attended it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meeting was held in November, as you can see in my documents. Mr. Praljak was cooperative in the course of our discussions. He said that he would do everything he could, that he would contact the local authorities up there in order to ensure that these people could return. These people did not return, and I can't say whether it's Mr. Praljak's fault or the fault of the local authorities in Prozor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just said that Mr. Praljak undertook to contact the local authorities. Did you witness any concrete steps taken by him or was -- was it only something that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I know is that no one returned. There were no results. As to whether Mr. Praljak did whatever he could or not, I really don't know because I didn't have access to such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you tell us, do you have an idea of whether people and to what extent such refugees did not want to return to Prozor or wanted to return but were not allowed and if they were not allowed, who refused the return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe you have the documents. As far as Prozor is concerned, most of the facilities, buildings that belonged to Muslims, had been destroyed, had been torched. Many of them didn't have anywhere to return to. Preparations would have had -- they would have had to make preparations so that people could return, and then there was political insecurity. No one could guarantee people's safety. There were both these elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that yesterday you said that you had spoken to the refugees. Did these refugees want to return or had they abandoned the idea of returning home for the reasons you have mentioned, that is to say because their houses had been destroyed or because the political conditions were not appropriate? When you spoke to these refugees, how did they feel? Did they want to stay in Jablanica, go elsewhere, or return to Prozor? How did you personally perceive their position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, naturally they wanted to return. Everyone would like to return home. But just a minute ago I said many had nowhere to return to because their homes had been destroyed, and political insecurity was such that it was difficult for them to return. They were more angry with us at the time. They were more angry with armija and the MUP in Jablanica than with the Croatian authorities because we didn't want to take revenge on the Croats, and this was almost more difficult for them than the fact that they had been expelled from up there. And I personally had a lot of problems as a result of this situation, as I have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if we could then, having touched further on that, can we then go again to the second meeting that you discussed, or proposed meeting that you had mentioned earlier this morning about meeting with Mr. Praljak in Tomislavgrad. Can you tell us who approached you about that meeting and what happened.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I may provide you with a brief explanation. It was in November and at the time the HVO openly requested that Jablanica join Herceg-Bosna. At the time I was in command of the armed forces in Jablanica, and after some hesitation, after much hesitation, someone who had been my friend up until that point in time, he was the director in the company during the pre-war period, the company that I worked in, and he said, almost in tears, Safet, everything's over here. There's nothing we can do. This territory is supposed to go to the Croats. We'll die in vain. There's no way for us to confront the situation, and he said that he and Ivan Rogic had agreed in -- that I should accompany them in secrecy, and we should go to Tomislavgrad to see Mr. Praljak to try and agree on how to surrender the municipality to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can tell us -- if you care to, sir, tell us the name of this individual who approached you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Omer Macic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, then go with Mr. Macic and Mr. Rogic, Ivan Rogic, to meet with Mr. Praljak in Tomislavgrad?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. I was in a state of shock for about five seconds, and then I soon came to my senses and told the man that Jablanica municipality was my municipality, just as it was the municipality of all the other citizens. I said that I hadn't received inheritance from my father for no -- I said I hadn't received any inheritance from my father, and I told him that he should think about what he said, that it was stupid. Naturally, he maintained his position, and since that point in time I haven't had any contact with that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned several times yesterday that a meeting with President Izetbegovic in Jablanica that you said others were involved in,, I think there was even some agreement in the courtroom that at one point Mr. Petkovic and some of the others were involved. Did that happen on approximately the 14th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell us more -- we finally now have come to this particular meeting. Can you tell the Judges how this meeting came about, what the purpose of this meeting was, and what happened.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of the meeting was to reach an agreement on raising the blockade of Sarajevo. Winter was approaching. The first time that -- winter was approaching while Sarajevo was under blockade. The situation was very difficult. We were trying to reach an agreement on attempting to break into Sarajevo from Mount Igman, or rather, to raise the blockade of Sarajevo. That was the purpose of the meeting. Mr. Petkovic attended it, and I believe that some of his associates also attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of that meeting, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Petkovic suggested to Izetbegovic that he should contact Ivica Rajic in Kiseljak. He was the HVO commander there, and he expressed the hope that we would provide assistance and I think he requested a plan for the action so that he could analyse it. I think that's how things went. And when we left the meeting we hoped that something would be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to the plan to relieve Sarajevo in a moment. Can I ask you to tell the Judges, please, was there a second meeting involving President Izetbegovic in Jablanica a couple of days later, on the 16th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These discussing concerned raising the blockade of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did President Izetbegovic on this second occasion, did he say anything about HVO claims that he, that is, President Izetbegovic, and Mate Boban had reached any sort of agreement?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are a lot of speculations about Izetbegovic and Boban having reached an agreement. The HVO members and our men said that an agreement had been reached about having cantons in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this confused us. And we asked Mr. Izetbegovic to provide us with certain explanations. He said that this had been discussed but that he hadn't signed any kind of an agreement with Boban. All these rumours on an agreement reached between the two of them were just speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sometime after the second meeting, then, was there an effort by the ABiH to relieve Sarajevo in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And -- sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An action had been planned and carried out. On the 20th of December, units from the 4th Corps participated in the action, on the whole, and part of the Foca Brigade, which was in the Trnovo sector at the time. Unfortunately, and mostly due to poor leadership in the Supreme Command staff at the forward command post in Igman and also due to the terrible weather at the time of the operation, this operation failed. 55 men were killed, and five of them were my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, following the meeting that you had had some several days earlier with Mr. Petkovic, can you tell the Judges, did the HVO participate or assist in this effort to relieve Sarajevo on the 20th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for intervening, but I believe that it would be useful if first of all the witness told us whether a request for assistance had been sent to anyone in the HVO, and perhaps he could clarify something else that he mentioned, namely that at the meeting with President Izetbegovic, Milivoj Petkovic requested a plan for the action to raise the blockade of Sarajevo. That means that up until that point in time the HVO Main Staff didn't -- hadn't participated in drawing up that plan and knew nothing about it either. I think that putting such questions to the witness would help us to understand the situation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I regret the testimony that counsel's now offered in front of the witness about what the HVO did or didn't do or had or didn't have at that time. I don't think that's appropriate. I think the state of the evidence was clearly as is reflected in the transcript, is that there had been a meeting with Mr. Petkovic on the 18th -- excuse me, on the 16th of December, 1992. It had been proposed that the action to relieve Sarajevo was specifically proposed to him at that time, and the witness said that he said he would consult with his -- with Grude or superiors as to what would happen. I think that's where it was left exactly by the witness. All I simply asked was: Did the HVO participate in the effort to relieve Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll be very precise. I'll say where this can be found in the transcript. It's page 9, lines 6 to 8. And the witness said literally that Petkovic said they should contact Ivica Rajic in Kiseljak. He expressed the hope that he would provide assistance, and the witness said, I think, that he requested a plan for the action so that he could analyse it. So that's the basis for my intervention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sir, according to what the Defence has just said, and according to what Mr. Scott said earlier on, we would like to know the following: What did Mr. Petkovic do, in fact? Did he say that it was necessary to contact Rajic, who was in Kiseljak, and then we could draw the conclusion that HVO was going to be part of a plan to raise the blockade of Sarajevo. Can you provide us with any additional information about what the various actors said and did, and this ties up with the question put to you by Mr. Scott, and I want to put it to you as well: Did the HVO participate in this unfortunate action? Did it participate effectively or did it provide logistics or equipment or men to assist with the plan for Sarajevo? Can you provide us with any other information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The HVO did not participate in the action. As to what happened after the meeting with Mr. Petkovic and Izetbegovic, well, naturally, I don't know anything about that. That's not something I could know about. Petkovic said that he wanted to be provided with a plan so that he could have a look at it, and he said -- or, rather, he told Mr. Izetbegovic that he should contact Rajic. As to what happened between them afterwards, I don't know. You shouldn't ask me about that because that's not something I could have known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are telling us that Mr. Petkovic wanted to know about a plan. As we're dealing with military matters, well, this seems quite logical. And I believe that you are saying that the plan he requested was not provided to him by the ABiH, and that could explain that the HVO didn't participate in an action in Sarajevo on the 20th of December. Is that how we are to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite possible. That's quite possible. I have told you that I didn't know what happened afterwards, but it's quite possible that Mr. Petkovic didn't receive the plan and that he didn't participate. Not a single serious commander would send his troops in if he didn't know where he was sending them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps in the course of the cross-examination, if Mr. Petkovic's Defence has other questions to put to you, they may do so. Mr. Scott, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Around this same time, sir, was there a meeting in Jablanica with some of the HVO or HDZ leaders where it was -- where they communicated what should happen with Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. There was a series of meetings in November and December, and they tried to persuade the municipality leadership to accept the structure of the HZ HB in Jablanica. It wasn't much of a meeting. I attended some; I didn't attend others. I didn't participate much in those meetings at the time because the issues were political rather than military. All these meetings ended without having obtained any results, but there was -- people hoped that they would meet again and discuss matters again. So they didn't want to close the door to cooperation. They wanted to continue discussing things. That was the purpose of the meetings. At the time, the HDZ, or rather, the HVO was openly trying to establish its authority. My position was that they should discuss things, that they should avoid fighting at all costs even if they had two power structures in place. And that was the way in which I tried to contribute to that work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: A couple of things to clarify, sir, if we can. Yesterday you mentioned that the three top or senior HVO or HDZ leaders in the Jablanica municipality were Mirko Zelenika, Ivan Rogic, and Matan Zaric. First of all, because there were two Zelenikas with very similar names, can you just confirm to the Judges, please, Mirko Zelenika is a different person than Marko Zelenika.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The two of them are brothers. Marko was an HVO commander and Mirko performed various duties. At the time he was perhaps the president of the Executive Board, and just before the conflict broke out I know that he worked in the MUP. So he was always present more or less. Marko was the commander or a commander. At the time that both of us performed such duties, not a single serious incident occurred in Jablanica. Whenever it was tense on either of the sides, we both went to deal with the matter. When refugees from Prozor arrived, when the tension was great, we walked around town together. We would sit down in places where large numbers of people had gathered in restaurants or bars or elsewhere. And we did that to show people that we weren't on opposite sides, that we were cooperating. Unfortunately, sometime in January, Marko was replaced, or perhaps it was at the beginning of February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know why Marko -- you've gone a bit ahead of it, but since you have, do you know why Marko Zelenika was removed or dismissed at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly why he was replaced. I only have assumptions, but I can't really tell you. I wasn't involved in appointment and replacement of officers. I can only have assumptions, but as to how relevant they are, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this --

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he wasn't radical enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask you, was he -- was Marko Zelenika, did you consider him much more of a moderate and helpful to you than his brother Mirko Zelenika?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Excuse me. If I may object here. Again, this -- the way the question is phrased I believe is unfair. It presupposes that one is different than the other. He can simply ask, you know, describe the differences as opposed to leading on the witness in that fashion. And for the record, he indicated he didn't want to speculate but then he speculated, but we'll deal with that on cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my question is quite straightforward. I followed up his -- what he did give, the answer he did give, and we can state it a different way, the difference in the political positions or philosophies, if you will, of the two brothers, and I've asked Mr. Idrizovic to tell us exactly that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did they hold different political views in your experience?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sorry, I don't want to belabour that and I'm sure if counsel wants to come back to it, they will. During the meetings that you said that you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give us more information about the differences that you observed between the two brothers? You said that Marko was replaced because he wasn't radical enough. Could we then conclude that his brother was far more radical in his views? Is there anything based on which we could see the difference between the role of one and the other? If you know, please tell us; otherwise, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in one of the minutes that I sent here, minutes of these bodies that were the decision-makers, the Presidency, and there is a quotation of Mirko's words, namely, that there are two authorities, one in Sarajevo and one in the other place; that he knew regulations of both authorities; and that the one in Sarajevo didn't really function and the other one did; and that generally our only possibility to communicate was via Herzegovina with Croatia, that there was no other way. And that based on that, he insisted that the municipality be placed under efficient control of the HVO. This is stated in the minutes that all of you have before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a brief question for you. Do you know exactly what is the name of the person who replaced Marko Zelenika from his military post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. That was the HVO staff, and now as to the level at which it was decided, I don't know that. I suppose that he was the main person in the Jablanica HVO staff. I don't really know their exact structure and chain of command in order to be able to tell you who exactly decided to replace him. At any rate, the lowest level at which this could have been done was the brigade command, Herceg Stjepan, within which this battalion that was in Jablanica existed, or perhaps somebody above him, commander of the operative zone or commander of the Main Staff. I assume that that would be the chain of command to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, let me go back to something that you mentioned earlier before my learned friend put a question to you. You said that Mirko Zelenika at a session said that there were two authorities: One which functioned, the one in Grude; and the other one which didn't, meaning the one in Sarajevo. You personally represented the military command in Jablanica. You were at the highest level, which is to say you were a person who had a good view of the events. Please tell me, this statement of Mr. Zelenika, was it consistent with the situation on the ground as you saw it? In other words, did you believe that the state authorities in Sarajevo were failing in performing their duties in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a good question. Sarajevo was under siege in 1992. The only communication went via the airport in Sarajevo, and the airport was at the demarcation line and it was guarded by the French soldiers. Any crossing of the runway could be deadly, and that was the only way to communicate with Sarajevo. There was no possibility for any proper technical links. It was difficult to maintain communication. The only efficient links that we had was via lines going to Kakanj and then to Sarajevo, and it was a very complicated link anyway. So to discuss any proper functioning of authorities in Sarajevo is really an illusion. This has more to do with legitimacy because there is an internationally recognised state; it has some sort of organs of power. As to their efficiency during wartime, it's hard to discuss it. Under those circumstances, we had to organise life at the local level. We didn't expect any major assistance, nor did we receive any. We were simply legalists. There was legal authority in Bosnia and then there were two other authorities that were illegal, which was the HVO and the Republika Srpska. We didn't feel any consequences of the HVO authority. The only communication we had with them was the permit that they would issue us to leave the territory. So you could leave the territory only if they allowed you to. They were issue -- they represented everything, the constitution, they issued passports, visas, everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you for this answer. We will discuss this further among us. Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Thank you for all that. Now, returning to these meetings you said there were a series of meetings in November/December 1992, and I had asked you about some of these individuals and that's how we began talking about Mirko Zelenika. And my follow-on question to you was to be: Did -- Mirko Zelenika and this other man you've mentioned several times, Matan Zaric, were they actively engaged in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they participated, of course. Most of those meetings, or rather, all of those meetings were held mostly at their initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges anything more than you already have? If you can, do so; if you can't, we'll move forward. Can you tell the Judges anything more about what Mr. Mirko Zelenika and Matan Zaric said at these meetings about the future of Jablanica municipality?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've already said that. They said that the authority in Sarajevo wasn't functioning properly, that the one in Grude did, that we had no communication with Sarajevo, and that we had to go down there. That was it. They wanted to place the municipality under the efficient control of the HVO, and that allegedly there would be no problems further on at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What do you mean by "there would be no problems further on"?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the organs of authority would be functioning. We would have communication with Croatia and then with the rest of the world. The life would be normal, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did the Muslim authorities and the ABiH in Jablanica accept the proposals by Mr. Mirko Zelenika and Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course not. We didn't accept them. The issue concerned legality. If we had accepted this structure, well, that would have meant no longer considering Bosnia and Herzegovina as our home. That was unacceptable for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's go on, please, then into January of 1993 and touch back on this man Daidza. Did you have any final dealings with Mr. Daidza in January 1993; and if so, tell the Judges what happened with that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in January 1993, at the time in mid-January the conflict in Central Bosnia and Gornji Vakuf had escalated again. And once again Daidza gave a demonstration of force, he acted arrogantly, he had spent a long period of time in the territory, but he was of absolutely no military use to us. He didn't go to the lines, he didn't participate in any actions, he would spread misinformation about the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and around the 20th of January, 1993, he disappeared. He was no longer seen in Jablanica until the end of the war. But we saw him later in Sarajevo as the military attache of the Croatian embassy in Sarajevo. Later he came to Sarajevo again but to feast on roast meat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, continuing on in January, can you tell the Judges whether anything happened in connection with the managers or directors of the electrical generation companies in Jablanica and surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think on the 9th, the 9th of January, that the appointment arrived for the director of the electrical industry of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and this was in our municipality, in part of the company for the Jablanica municipality. It was an attempt to take over and place under HVO control what was most valuable; that was the power industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit 1088.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that a document -- an HVO document that indicates what happened around that time that you just told us about?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document of the Elektroprivreda company of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and their decree on appointment of persons into the units for Jablanica, the Jablanica power-plant, and all the facilities that the company covered, and some of them were located in Jablanica, for the maintenance of the hydro-electric power-station, or rather, pertaining to the decision on establishment of the public company Elektroprivreda and so on as the document reads.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may interrupt here for a second. The Prosecution has indicated that this is an HVO document. Perhaps the witness can indicate to us how is it that this is an HVO document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me first correct myself, Your Honour. I should have used "Herceg-Bosna" as opposed to "HVO." Other than that, I'll certainly let the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you clarify that in response to counsel's question, Mr. Idrizovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, ask the witness what the document is and from where it is, and I think if we look at the names that might help us a little bit as well, and the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's my -- Mr. Karnavas and I are not in disagreement on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you look at the top of the letter-head, if you will, sir, and indicate from whom this company -- excuse me, from whom this correspondence or decree came. I think everyone in the courtroom can read it.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that. I did -- I said it was not from the HVO but from the public enterprise called Elektroprivreda of Herceg-Bosna, and that, of course, was formed by the HVO, the Elektroprivreda of Herceg-Bosna company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, did there come a time around the middle of January 1993 that you received some order or information that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. You're confusing us. You've just said that this company was set up by the HVO. I understood it that this enterprise was a state enterprise. So could you clarify that point, please. This electrical company, did it exist before the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it did exist as a public enterprise, the Elektroprivreda of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is before the war. Now, during the war the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna established from a part of that company, took over a part of that company, that was under its control and set up the public enterprise of Elektroprivreda Herceg-Bosna. May I be allowed to finish?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it set up this public enterprise, was there a document about its establishment or was it a de facto establishment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know that. They had very effective control over the hydro-electric power-station Rama and I think Mostar as well, and Salakovac probably. There were five electrical power stations in that series, and during the war the situation changed. Some would go from the hands of the Serbs into the control of the Croats then under Muslim control. They changed hands, moved around. So from one enterprise that existed before the war, two were formed. You had the part that was controlled by the BH army, that was linked to Sarajevo; and the other section was under HVO control, and they set up their public enterprise, and it was the Elektroprivreda of the HZ HB. Now, what we're talking about now is an attempt to have the Elektroprivreda Herceg-Bosna take over those sections of the enterprise that were under the control of the BH army. So that's what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. President, just a couple of points of clarification. One, if he could read whether -- in his own language where it says "decree," it's my understanding that a misinterpretation. It's a decision. If we can clarify that. Also, you may wish to ask the gentleman regarding the names. We see several names here, you know, of what ethnicity or nationality they're from, because I think that would be quite revealing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sir, could you read in your own language the title in capital letters, italics, before the preamble, or rather, the part before the preamble and after paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a decision, "rjesenje," on appointment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it's a decision. Now, the people who were appointed, could you read their names out for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Omer Macic, Salih Islamovic, Jure Tadic, Uzeir Muratovic, Ivica Cule, Davorin Sunjic, Junuz Vejzovic, and Zulfo Rebovic twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Now, I have a follow-up question now. I understood you to say that this enterprise in fact was under the control of the ABiH and that this document attests to the fact that the HVO wanted to place the company under its control. Is that what you told us or not, or did I understand you incorrectly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the control of the authorities in Sarajevo was part of this enterprise, part of it was under that control; another part of it was already under HVO control. And this is an attempt to place the whole enterprise under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's quite clear now. Yes, another question from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may ask a question. Looking at these names, can you tell us whether they are typically Croat names or whether they are Muslim names or can it not be seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you can tell everything. There are Muslims and Croats here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the record, all three from Jablanica are from -- are Muslim. I think that's an important -- since we're talking about Jablanica, a point not to be missed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Can you confirm that, Witness, the number 1, I think; 2, at any rate; and 4, these are persons from Jablanica and they are all Muslims. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A last question from the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said several times part of the enterprise was in the hands of the HVO and another part of it was in the hands of the BiH. What do you mean by "a part"? The enterprise was divided in two, in fact, and each part was autonomous and produced electricity in an autonomous manner, independent manner. Is that the explanation or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is a partial explanation. This is what that's about. This was the system at one point; that's how it worked. It was all linked up, or rather, it was all the system of Elektroprivreda, the electrical distribution system of Yugoslavia as a whole, and you couldn't look at one hydro-electric power-plant on its own without looking at all the others, because you have an electricity network. Electricity forms a network. You don't get electricity from one hydro-electric power-station to one particular town. You have a whole electricity network that supplies power for the whole country. Now, we have Jablanica were not able to send electricity to Sarajevo, for example, or anywhere else because the long-distance transmission lines had been destroyed. Now, the people from Herceg-Bosna, for example, for the most part were able to, but only together with us, because the main equipment was located in Jablanica. So to send electricity towards Croatia and western Herzegovina. Technical facilities existed for that; that was feasible. So if I don't -- I'm not going to take up too much of your time, let me say that the electric power-station of Jablanica was 150 megawatts in size, and throughout the war it worked with only 2 megawatts, because we in Jablanica and the surrounding parts where the network existed were able to use up that much energy, and that was below all the technical norms, standards, of work. So the aim was for the electricity produced in the hydro-electric power plants on the River Neretva, all of them, I'm speaking in general terms now, be redirected towards Croatia or western Herzegovina, because there was no possibility of us sending it out to Sarajevo and further afield to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, is one to understand that the Jablanica power-plant had a strategic position in the diffusion and distribution of electrical energy to Mostar and Croatia? And does that mean that if your power-plant wasn't functioning, wasn't operational or had been destroyed, there were important consequences for other regions, Mostar, for instance, or Croatia? Would that be right? Or, in a word, was the power-plant there crucial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that power-plant itself was one of the five electrical power stations that were the most important ones. But it wasn't the problem in the power-plant; the problem was in the whole system of transporting electrical energy, which went from Jablanica, not from this particular power-plant, but from another large facility, switching facility, which went towards Rastani and Mostar and so on, then towards Sarajevo, Kakanj, Zagreb. Now, what kind of system this was, well, the electricity from Salakovac, Grabovica, Jablanica, and Rama, those power-plants would come to that switching facility and then was further distributed where it was meant to go, and this system was furnished for the former Yugoslavia. It was built to cater to the former Yugoslavia. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what you're saying is that this transport system for electricity is important, not the power-plant that just produced 2 megawatts instead of producing 1.500 milliwatts, but it was the system of transporting that electricity. Now, starting out from that, if the transporting system was not working in Jablanica, does that mean that all the electricity produced, if we look at Bosnia, Croatia, and if we look at what is happening in recent times, was paralysed if the Jablanica plant was not properly functioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that would be partly true, yes. Jablanica, the hydro-electric power-plant of Jablanica was always able to produce 150 megawatts if it had what to produce it with. The watt problem wasn't in producing it; it was in consumption. So the power we produced, we didn't have anybody to give it to. Now, if it was part of the Elektrobosna capacity, it could work at full capacity and send out electricity towards western Herzegovina and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Praljak is going to tell us that he's an electrical engineer. What question is it that you want to ask, Mr. Praljak? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Well, with your permission I'd like to ask a few questions of the witness and try and clarify the problem in that way, with the Court's indulgence and permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can ask your questions in the cross-examination because otherwise Mr. Scott is going to be very angry because we've taken up all his time. Having said that, continue, Mr. Scott. We're going to throw light on the issue, I'm absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I'd like to turn out the light on that issue and go forward, if we could. I think that we have all learned enough about the electrical network in Herzegovina and Bosnia to know -- probably to have some appreciation for the importance of these facilities. I think that's sufficient. And I'll leave it to counsel and Mr. Praljak if they care to take us further into the dynamics of the manufacture and distribution of electrical power.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you please tell us, did there come a time in January, mid-January 1993 where you received a decision or order that the ABiH forces were to submit themselves or subordinate themselves to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing. What would happen? We received an order from the defence minister, it was read out through the information media, that the units of the ABiH in the cantons, which at the time was supposed to be Croatian according to that famous Vance-Owen Plan, that they should be resubordinated to the HVO or moved. That was the purpose of the order. That's what it said. We -- but we didn't act upon it, but that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges a bit more about how this decision or order came to you; who issued it; what, if any, communications you had about it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. Just one brief intervention for the record. I think that it is important. Page 28, line 15, it should have -- the words "we didn't take it seriously" should have been recorded. That's what he said. "We didn't take it seriously."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. I think that's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me go back to my question, though. Can you tell us more about who issued this decision or at least communicated it to you?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a decision by the defence minister of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Bozo Rajic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now -- excuse me. Can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit 1164. Can you tell us about that document, sir.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it describes what we were speaking about a moment ago, that the Jablanica inhabitants can't leave the municipality without a permit issued by the authorities, and it is signed and stamped, Ivan Zatica [as interpreted], Ivan Rogic, and Marko Zelenika and for the procurement of goods, purchase of goods, other people, probably those who went to pick up the goods, had to pay a duty on them. When it was military equipment, military equipment could be brought in with only permission of Milivoj Petkovic, it says, Ante Jelavic, et cetera, and Bruno Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just because the English translation may not be clear or correct, can I ask you to look in particular at paragraph number 3 of the Bosnian language version of the document. And where the English language says something, and I'm just simply going to try to be as neutral as possible, it says one of the names at the end of the paragraph 3, it says Milivoj and then CIG, if you look in the Bosnian language original of that document, can you see that name, sir?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic, or Mr. Ante Jelavic, assistant for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Now, unless there's questions about that document, I'm moving on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, (i) says that the document is to be signed by Zaric, Rogic, and Marko Zelenika. Now, in the B/C/S document, which has been photocopied, the photocopy of the document, I understood you to say that their signatures were there. Is that right? Because in the English translation it would appear that it was just the chief of the military police who signed the document, but do you recognise the signature on the document of Mr. Rogic in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was signed by Stojan Livaja, military police chief, or commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, so that's the only signature on the document. Is there no other signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no other signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wanted that to be cleared up. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, did -- in January of 1993, were you asked to form another military formation in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what that was all about. We're dealing with January. This wasn't any conflict with the HVO, or at least they weren't planned, we didn't plan them. So the concept for the further development of the army was to establish manoeuvre units capable of carrying out combat operations outside the territory in which they were formed. And at that time, we were faced with a very difficult situation linked to the siege of Sarajevo and the siege of Gorazde and the very difficult problems that eastern Herzegovina and Foca were facing. And at the time in Jablanica, we had more than 10.000 refugees. From those parts in a town which had 3.000 inhabitants previously, there was suddenly 10.000 refugees. Commander Pasalic issued an order to form a brigade, and that in the shortest space of time possible, it should be capacitated to carry out combat operations outside the territory of the municipality. The brigades had already been formed in Mostar, Konjic, and this process was to be completed in Jablanica too. I did that, and mostly all the young population and command staff, younger men and command staff, were deployed in a brigade, and on the 21st of January, officially it came into existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, is this the unit then that was the ABiH 44th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later on it was to be called the 44th, but when it was established it was called the Neretva Brigade, and later on all those brigades pursuant to a corps order were to receive numbers. The 4th Corps -- the first number of all the brigades was a 4, the digit 4, and then it said Mostar unit, the eastern Herzegovina unit, the Stolac unit. 30 was the Konjic establishment. The fourth was us. The fifth was the Neretva river valley, and so on, the 45th and so on. So when they were -- it was established it was called the Neretva Brigade, but it bore that name for a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when that was formed, sir, who became the commander of what shortly became the 44th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the brigade was Enes Kovacevic; he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And once this brigade was created in place, did you have any other involvement with the operations or command of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. I remained staff commander, but I had under my authority the units which provided security for the key facilities, vital facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About -- I had 200 members between 50 and 60 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question. Why didn't you become the commander of the 44th Brigade? What merits did Mr. Enes Kovacevic have over you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Enes used to work together with me in the Municipal Staff. He was much younger than me. Already at that time I was 44 years old, and otherwise it was the younger people that formed the brigade, made part of the brigade. I discussed this with my commander, corps commander, Pasalic, and he told me that I should stay in Jablanica and that the brigade was supposed to go on assignment outside the municipality, somewhere in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to finish on that, sir, if we could. So when Mr. Kovacevic was appointed as commander of the 44th Brigade, mountain brigade, if we can just use that terminology to distinguish that unit, who was his then-commanding officer or superior officer in his chain of command?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the corps commander, of course, Mr. Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then you said a moment ago that your responsibilities at that time then became the -- providing security -- it may have -- I think you said the words "key facilities, vital facilities," at line 5, page 32, in the Jablanica municipality and that you said you had about 200 men to participate in that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in looking in the transcript - I see it's about to leave the page - but you said "between 50 and 60." And when you said "between 50 and 60," you meant, is it correct, that the ages of these approximately 200 men were between the ages of 50 and 60?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Elderly people who were no longer fit for brigade work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, not so elderly, sir, let's -- it's less elderly all the time. Were these considered to be combat troops, sir, in any sense?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. They provided security for the facilities. Since we didn't have any weapons, they were mostly armed with the classical type of M-48 rifles that we had. We didn't have any automatic weapons for them. They weren't well equipped or trained or armed or anything like that for them to be able to carry out any serious combat assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm about to change the -- move now going to April 1993, and I wonder if that might be the time to take the morning break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 10.25. We're going to take a 20-minute break and reconvene at quarter to 10.00 -- 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Idrizovic, I had -- I received some comment during the break that perhaps one or two of your last answers were not entirely clear. I think perhaps they were, but just to be sure. When you're talking about the 200 men aged between approximately 50 and 60 years old, this is the -- is it correct that that was the, I'm going to call it, the security unit that was then under your command for the purpose of protecting or guarding various facilities in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And then what we've been calling today and what became the 44th Mountain Brigade was an entirely separate military unit that you no longer had any responsibility for. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Moving forward then to the -- early April 1993. Can you tell the Judges, please, did you observe any changes in the HVO forces in Jablanica town, any changes in where they were located or their movements?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The HVO headquarters was not even a hundred metres away from my command. In the second half of April, one could notice that there were fewer and fewer HVO members in the command and in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you know the people that were leaving, and you said it was fewer and fewer, do you know where these people, other HVO members, soldiers, were going at the time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the village of Doljani, which was in the western part of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you to look, please, at Exhibit 2487. Sir, this is a document from the HVO Herceg Stjepan Brigade dated the 22nd of May, 1993. Could I please direct your attention to about the -- approximately maybe the fifth paragraph of that document where if you can find the words, please, "after all that, the HVO decided to transfer its units to Doljani."

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that in fact consistent with what you told us a moment ago, this is what you saw happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you a couple of other questions --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it would be very good to see what is concealed behind the word "after all of that," or rather, have a look at the preceding paragraph to see why the HVO decided to move to Doljani. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, with great respect for my good friend, I mean, the document is there. Everyone has it in the courtroom. There's no effort to conceal anything from the Chamber. The Chamber can read the document. If counsel wants to go into further details on cross-examination, she's fully entitled to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is an issue that could be raised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask you to look at the next paragraph to the one I directed your attention to previously, there's a -- it starts: "On the 14th of April, 1993, Croats were banned from entering Jablanica for regular work." Can you tell the Judges whether that paragraph is -- based on your observation, experience, is what that says true?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I've mixed something up. Could you provide me with the document number, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, of course. 2487. It may be in the second binder if you don't have it, you've lost it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, could you assist the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, but could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Sir, directing your attention -- I directed your attention a moment ago to the paragraph that talks about the HVO units or HVO decision to transfer its units to Doljani village. The next paragraph says: "On 14 April 1993, Croats were banned from entering Jablanica for regular work." Now, I'd like you to look at that paragraph, please, that's just -- is that statement true based on what you saw happening in Jablanica and the surrounding area at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this isn't true. As of the 13th of April, from Kostajnica and Falanovo hill in the Ostrozac sector in the direction of Konjic, a road had been blocked. Fire had been opened to block this road, so we were completely cut off from Konjic. So during that period it wasn't possible to leave Jablanica. This road was under fire in the Ostrozac sector on the opposite side beyond the lake, and whoever was in Jablanica just had to stay there. It wasn't possible to leave Jablanica. No one even attempted to do so. Life had come to a standstill. So during that period of time until the road was opened up again, we were completely encircled. Clashes broke out in the Neretvica part of the municipality of Konjic, it's called Neretvica or Klis, it depends, so at that time we were completely isolated. The blockade imposed on us was complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have several follow-up questions, sir. When you said a few moments ago -- a moment ago you said "this road was under fire, "the road in the Ostrozac sector," as I read it here if I've mispronounced it. Ostrozac perhaps.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Under fire from who?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under HVO fire from their positions at the Falanovo hill and further up, Radosine, Obri. That's in the area of Konjic municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you also said a moment ago that "the blockade imposed on us was complete," the blockade imposed by who?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the HVO imposed this blockade, and it was in the area of Konjic municipality Ostrozac was our only territory. In the area of Ostrozac and further on towards Konjic the blockade was complete. It wasn't possible to budge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how long did that blockade continue?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it lasted for over a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before we leave this document, on the next -- in the next paragraph, it's not clear it may be -- well, in the next paragraph then you see the words: "After that, Croats in the Doljani area were blockaded by members of the Independent Battalion of the Army of the RBH." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. In the area of Doljani and Sovici we had a total of about 120 or 130 soldiers, most of them were in Sovici. We knew that if a conflict between the armija and the HVO broke out, these units would just not be able to put up resistance. Their exclusive task was to get the population out in the direction of Jablanica if a conflict broke out; that's why these units had been established and that's the only reason. Once the conflict had broken out, the commanders from Doljani acted on their instructions. They got their people out. They evacuated the people, so there were no victims in Doljani. Unfortunately, the commander who was in Sovici fell for an HVO trick when they attacked Sovici and he surrendered. They said that if they surrendered -- well, they said they should surrender and then the people suffered the fate they suffered. I wouldn't like to go into that now. Other direct participants of those events could tell you about this. The civilian population was expelled, so there was no reason not to get the people from Sovici out. There were no obstacles to that. That was to the far west of our municipality, and there was this area inhabited by Croats alone, and they were in an unfortunate position because one year earlier in the area of Strop, Sovicka Vrata, Borovik, Borovac, there were HVO positions there on the Pisvir mountain. So a year prior to this conflict that entire area had been taken over by the HVO. No one serious would have suggested that people fight there or that they attack someone because they'd already been encircled. So their only task was to save the population, and this man in Sovici didn't do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir, perhaps it's clear now from what you just said. But earlier you said "they were in an unfortunate position." And just so the record is clear, when you say "they were in an unfortunate position," who were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the members of the armija in Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you come to believe around this same time, around the 13th and 14th of April, 1993, that Jablanica town itself was under threat of attack?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the town of Jablanica had been under threat since April 1992. I think I've already said this. I think I said yesterday in April and May 1992 all the important elevations to the west and to the south, but mostly to the west, had been taken by the HVO. I'm referring to the Boksevica mountain above Ostrozac to the Pisvir mountain above Doljani and Slatina, and then there's Strop, Sovicka Vrata, not to mention the units at Risovac, and there were many of them there. We had contact with HVO officers at the time and pointed this out, and they kept saying that that was a third defence line facing the Serbs, although the Serbs were very far away. There were no Serbs in the vicinity. And that was a sort of obstacle to our cooperation. We had already been blocked off, cut off, and we could see where their positions were. Naturally in May or June some kind of an army had been established by then. We were able to drive those people away or try to do that, but our leadership never allowed us to do this because they didn't want us to spoil our relationship, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you back then to the 14th of April, 1993, and when you believed that an attack on Jablanica might be imminent, were any efforts made by the authorities in Jablanica, the Muslim authorities in Jablanica, if you will, to contact or have talks with the HVO authorities?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that on the 15th in the morning immediately prior to the attack, representatives from our brigade and representatives of the authorities went to discuss things in Doljani together with UNPROFOR representatives, and naturally there were no agreements -- no agreement was reached. On the way to Jablanica, the shelling of the town started; that was on the 15th of April at about quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Before we touch further on the shelling of the town of Jablanica, did you understand that two of the HVO or HDZ officials that the Jablanica representatives met with were Matan Zaric and Stipe Pole?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question isn't precise. I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies. You told us a moment ago that a group of representatives went from Jablanica to Doljani to meet with representatives of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did the HVO participants in that meeting include Mr. Zaric and Mr. Pole?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in the shelling that then began as the Muslim representatives were returning from Doljani, how long did the shelling of Jablanica town continue?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it continued throughout the day. Sometimes it was more intensive, sometimes less intensive, but it affected various parts of the municipality. The town was shelled, part of the Gornje Papratsko village or the area of the Gornje Papratsko village, then the Podrinje villages, that's what they are called. The shelling was random throughout the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit 1903. If I can ask you, please, to look at paragraph number 2 of that document. Does that again indicate and is it consistent with your testimony that HVO units and part of the civilians had been pulled out to Doljani? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is -- going to paragraph number 3, is it also consistent with your testimony just now that on the 14th and 15th of April there were meetings in Doljani in which also some international representatives were involved?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there, in fact, any sort of a radio correspondent in Jablanica around this time, this is covered in paragraph number 1, named Fazlo Dervisbegovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit 2133. Did anything -- or was anything said to you or did you hear around this time that there had been some alleged joint statement signed by Izetbegovic and Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally there were rumours about this. HVO representatives said that this agreement had been signed. Naturally we didn't have any written evidence to that effect. And I think that at some point yesterday I said that when we had direct contact with Izetbegovic, when he came to Jablanica, we put this question to him. And he said that no agreement had been reached, that nothing had been signed, and it was pure speculation on the part of the HVO when they said that an agreement had been signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, which date are we talking about? When -- how many times has Mr. Izetbegovic come now, because I want to make sure that we're precise, because this would be the second time that Izetbegovic is there and I guess Izetbegovic was still his host at that occasion as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honour, I don't think that's correct, in fairness to Mr. Karnavas and, both, the witness. I think the witness just said that he made earlier -- he made reference to an earlier conversation. He didn't say that Mr. Izetbegovic was in Jablanica on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I take it, so the record is clear, that on the -- in -- on the 2nd of April or so, 1993, Mr. Izetbegovic was not in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't remember him being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And then was there an -- did an armed conflict then break out in the area of Sovici-Doljani during this time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as we are concerned -- THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps we could establish the date in the Croatian text and the English text. In the Croatian text, it says that it was signed on the 20th of April in Zagreb; and in the English text it says 2 question mark April. So it's not the 2nd of April, it's the 25th of April, the 25th of April in Zagreb, signed by Izetbegovic and Boban. And in the translation you have -- it says the 2nd of April. I think that's a serious mistake. It's the 25th of April. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree with that. I'm sorry, I misspoke, and Mr. Petkovic is correct. I believe the copy is very bad, but I believe -- I believe it is either the 24th or the 25th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, around this time, did the -- did an armed conflict break out in the areas of Doljani and Sovici?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we are concerned, the conflict broke out on the 15th of April when the shelling of Jablanica started. After that date, after our representatives in -- had been in Doljani, we no longer had any contact with that area. There was no link to the area of any kind. It was only when refugees from that area arrived that we found out about what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did in fact some people, refugees or persons who had escaped from the armed conflict, did come from these villages to Jablanica town?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they all came from Doljani, and very small number of people came from Sovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you involved around this time, then, in a meeting with some international organisations, including UNPROFOR, in an effort to determine what was happening or what had happened in this area?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Meetings were held in relation to that issue. At the time I didn't go to Doljani, but members from our brigade went there together with the HVO members. And our corps commander also went there, Mr. Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And we'll come back to Sovici and Doljani in a moment. But during this time, was there also an attack continuing -- or attacks, from time to time continuing on Jablanica town?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never ceased. The shelling of the town was carried out on a daily basis, and 35 civilians were killed as a result of the shelling, and 10 of these civilians were children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you become aware around this same time of any fighting around the villages of Parcani, Paros, Klek, Skrobucani?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A few refugees came to Jablanica from those villages and talked about it, told us about it. They said that in a boat when they were trying to escape over the lake of Rama that four of their soldiers disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did they tell you what had happened in those villages?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the villages were attacked according to the same model and the population expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit 1952. In this report it indicates that there was an action -- there were -- yeah, there was an action concerning these Muslim villages, Parcani, Paros, Klek, and Skrobucani. Is what's stated here consistent with what you understood and heard at the time from the people coming from those villages?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, did it come to your attention later in April that apparently there had been some sort of a cease-fire put in place involving, among others perhaps, Mr. Halilovic and Mr. Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there were orders to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to look at Exhibit 2037.

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is the call for the cessation of hostilities indicated in this document consistent with what you saw happening in the area at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think we received a similar order from our own commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was the Mijat Tomic Battalion of the HVO, was that one of the principal units in the Sovici -- HVO units in the Sovici-Doljani area?

utterances.speaker: SAFET IDRIZOVIC [Resumed]
